lesson.title: In a Different Voice: Gilligan's Challenge to Kohlberg
lesson.summary: Carol Gilligan argued that Kohlberg's model of moral development, built from research on boys and men, overemphasized abstract justice reasoning and gave too little credit to a care based moral orientation centered on relationships and responsibility.
lesson.body:
Carol Gilligan worked closely with Lawrence Kohlberg and noticed something that troubled her about his research: the longitudinal study his stage model was originally built on followed only boys. When Gilligan listened closely to how women and girls talked through moral dilemmas in her own interviews, she heard a recognizable and coherent way of reasoning that did not always score as highly on Kohlberg's scale, not because it was less sophisticated, she argued, but because it emphasized different values, relationships, responsibility to specific people, and avoiding harm to those connections, that Kohlberg's scoring system, built around abstract rights and justice, was not designed to fully credit.

Gilligan laid out this argument in her influential 1982 book, In a Different Voice, proposing an ethic of care as a legitimate and mature form of moral reasoning distinct from, not beneath, the justice oriented reasoning Kohlberg's stages were built to detect. Where a justice orientation asks what is fair or what rule applies, a care orientation asks who will be hurt and how relationships and responsibilities to specific people should be honored. Her point was not that one orientation is better than the other, but that a model claiming to describe moral maturity in general should not be built exclusively around one of them.

It is worth being careful about what Gilligan's research does and does not establish. Her claim was not that all women reason through care and all men reason through justice; later research testing whether there is a large, consistent gender difference in care versus justice orientation has produced mixed results, with many studies finding that both men and women draw on both kinds of reasoning depending on the situation. What has held up well, and what makes her critique lasting, is the more basic methodological point: a developmental model built from a single group's responses risks mistaking that group's typical style of reasoning for the definition of maturity itself.

Read together, Kohlberg and Gilligan are best understood not as a right answer and a wrong answer but as two lenses on moral reasoning that expand on each other, one centered on abstract fairness and rights, the other on relationships and care, both of which show up in how real people actually reason through hard moral questions.
